Pandemic vs Forbidden Island: Which Co-Op?

2026-11-11

Pandemic vs Forbidden Island is the same designer asking the same question twice, and the answer he gave each time is different. Both are cooperative. Both are Matt Leacock. One costs $44.43, the other $20.99.

If you want the answer with no scrolling: buy Forbidden Island if you are teaching a table that has never played a cooperative game, or you want to spend $21 instead of $44. Buy Pandemic if your group already plays games and wants the version with more to hold in your head.

Both play 2 to 4 players. Both are in my collection. The difference is not difficulty in the sense of "harder to win." It is how many things you have to track at once, and that decides which table each one belongs on.

What They Share

Start with how much is genuinely identical, because it is more than people expect.

Both are cooperative: everyone wins or everyone loses, and there is no traitor. Both put you in a fixed number of roles with a special ability. Both run on a deck that acts as a clock, and in both games that clock is the real opponent. Both scale on the same dial, which is how many cards the clock burns.

Both are also quarterback-able. That is the standard complaint about cooperative games and it is honest here: one player who knows the game well can run the whole table if you let them. Forbidden Island makes that harder than Pandemic does, for a reason worth knowing.

The Number That Separates Them

Pandemic asks you to track four diseases, each with a cure and an eradication state. You are managing a hand of cards toward four separate sets, watching two separate loss conditions, and moving around a map that connects in different ways in different cities.

Forbidden Island asks you to collect four treasures and get everyone off the island. It has one loss condition you have to watch in two places, and the island itself is a shrinking map you can see at a glance.

That is the whole comparison. Pandemic has roughly twice as many things in the air, and its complexity rating reflects that: 2.5 for Pandemic against 1.7 for Forbidden Island, on the standard scale where most family games sit under 2.

The Shelf Test

Here is the test I use when a game is this close on paper. Which one do you reach for when the table is mixed, some people know the game and some do not?

Forbidden Island wins that. The board tells everyone what is happening. You can see the island sinking, you can see which tiles are flooded, and a first-time player can make a real decision without being told what the right move is. The 30-minute play time means a loss does not cost you the evening, so losing does not create the tension that makes a group blame each other.

Pandemic loses that test, and it is not a flaw. The four-disease board is exactly what experienced players want: more to weigh, more ways a turn can matter, and a loss you can usually trace back to one specific decision. That is a better game for a group that plays together regularly. It is a worse game for a group that is learning together.

One honest thing: the quarterback problem is worse in Pandemic because there is more to be right about. If you are the person who sees the optimal line, you have to actively shut up, or you will play the game by yourself with three spectators.

Where Each One Belongs

Buy Forbidden Island ($20.99) if you are introducing cooperative games, playing with kids around 10, or you want a 30-minute game that fits after dinner. At this price it is the cheapest real co-op in the hobby, and it shares a designer with the one everyone recommends.

Buy Pandemic ($44.43) if your group already enjoys heavier games and wants a co-op with a real chance of a memorable loss. It is the game that made cooperative play mainstream for a reason, and 7.6 against 7.1 is a fair gap.

Buy both eventually. Forbidden Island is the teaching game, Pandemic is the next step, and together they cost less than one mid-weight strategy box.
